To snivel means to cry, whimper, or complain in a weak, pathetic, and self-pitying way — usually with sniffling and a runny nose involved. Think of a child who didn't get what they wanted and is now making a fuss about it in the most irritating, weepy way possible. That's sniveling.
The Two Sides of the Word

The verb snivel works on two levels that are tightly connected:

The physical side: Sniveling involves the actual, messy act of crying — with sniffling, a dripping nose, and whimpering. It's not clean, quiet, or dignified crying. It's the sloppy, noisy kind where someone can barely speak between sniffs.

The behavioral side: Sniveling also means to complain, whine, or moan about something in a feeble, self-pitying way — as if the person is a helpless victim who refuses to pull themselves together. Even without actual tears, someone can snivel just by whining and moaning pathetically.

In real use, these two sides often appear together — a person sniveling is typically both physically tearful and behaviorally pathetic at the same time.
The Crucial Part: What the Word Implies

This is where snivel becomes very interesting and precise. It is not a neutral word. It carries a strong sense of contempt and irritation from the person observing or describing the behavior.

When you say someone is sniveling, you are not just describing what they are doing — you are judging them for it. You are saying:

  • Their crying or complaining is not justified or is massively exaggerated.
  • They are being childishly weak and failing to show any backbone.
  • Their behavior is annoying and pitiable, not moving or sympathetic.
  • They are wallowing in self-pity instead of doing something useful.

This is a key distinction. If someone has lost a loved one and weeps deeply, you would never call that sniveling — that would be cruel and wrong. Sniveling is reserved for situations where the person's reaction seems weak, excessive, or unwarranted.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding snivel becomes much sharper when you place it next to related words:

Cry is completely neutral. It simply states a fact. "She cried at the movie." No judgment, no tone.

Weep is actually somewhat dignified. It suggests deep, genuine, heartfelt emotion. You weep for things that truly matter.

Sob is intense and genuine. A person sobbing is overwhelmed by real grief or pain. There's no mockery in calling someone's reaction "sobbing."

Whine is close to snivel but is more purely verbal — it focuses on complaining without necessarily involving tears. Snivel adds the physical, tearful, sniffly element on top of the whining quality.

Snivel sits at the lowest and most contemptuous end of this scale. It combines weakness, self-pity, tears, sniffling, and whining all at once — and it frames all of it as something unworthy of respect.
Who Uses This Word and When

Snivel is most commonly used when someone wants to tell another person — directly or indirectly — to stop being so pathetically weak and get on with things. It is frequently used:

  • By a stern or impatient person toward someone they think is overreacting: "Stop sniveling and get up."
  • To describe someone's behavior with obvious disapproval: "He spent the whole meeting sniveling about how unfair his workload was."
  • In a military, disciplinary, or tough-love context, where weakness is not tolerated.

It can be said directly to someone's face as a sharp command, or it can be used in the third person to describe someone behind their back — either way, the contempt is always present.

Snivel is not a word you'd find in a formal academic essay or an official report. It belongs to everyday spoken or written language, and it leans toward the informal side. You might find it in novels, conversation, opinion writing, or anywhere a writer wants to express contempt for weakness in a vivid and expressive way.
Putting It All Together With Examples

• "The soldier was told to stop sniveling and carry on with his duties." — Here the officer is dismissing the soldier's crying/complaining as unacceptable weakness.
  • "She sniveled into her sleeve, complaining that nobody ever helped her." — A picture of someone physically crying and sniffling while also whining and feeling sorry for themselves.
  • "I don't want to hear any more sniveling about how hard the exam was — everyone found it hard." — Used to shut down pathetic, self-pitying complaints.
  • "He sat in the corner sniveling while the rest of the team worked to fix the problem." — Paints someone as useless and weak while others show strength.

If you had to carry just one sentence in your memory, make it this: To snivel is to cry, sniffle, or complain in a weak and self-pitying way that other people find irritating, pathetic, and undeserving of sympathy.
